title: Debian doesn't boot anymore "error: file `/vmlinuz-6.12.113+deb13-amd64' not found" after kernel upgrade error due to missing space on /boot
body: I had the error zstd: error 70 : Write error : cannot write block : No space left on device again when trying to upgrade the kernel. I then freed up some space on that partition by moving the initrd.img and vmlinuz files temporarily out of it since I already had deleted all kernel files that aren't the running kernel or the new kernel and that didn't suffice. sudo apt-get upgrade then showed 0 packages to upgrade. When trying to boot to enter the grub password I get: error: file `/vmlinuz-6.12.113+deb13-amd64' not found error: you need to load the kernel first The disk is fully encrypted with LUKS and it uses UEFI. I have set a GRUB password. I can't select a previous kernel version to boot from in GRUB (there seems to be none left since I had to free space on /boot). How to repair this so it boots again? I know my /boot partition is a bit too small but I can't easily increase its size now.

title: do-release-upgrade insufficient disk space workaround
body: do-release-upgrade checks if there’s enough disk space to complete the release upgrade, in my case to 26.04. If it finds that there isn’t enough, it quits and asks you to free some space, then try again. In my case, there’s not too much I can delete. Also, I have only one partition, so linking space on the home partition to /var/cache/apt won’t work. AI suggested that I mount a USB and link to that, and although it seems that it should work, it just doesn’t. I suspect what is going on is that do-release-upgrade blindly checks the root partition, which hasn’t grown one bit because of this trick. It doesn’t realize that all these temporary.deb files will go to the USB, and therefore not fill up the root partition. And AI doesn’t realize this, and incorrectly assumes that a simple link will solve the problem. The second thing that AI suggested was to pass a -o option to do-release-upgrade, overriding the name of the apt cache directory. At first glance, one would think that this will work. In fact, it does work for apt-get. The .deb files land on the USB drive, and the light even flashes to give the user a sense of security. But it doesn’t work with do-release-upgrade. The light never illuminates, and the upgrade fails yet again. AI is quick to explain that do-release-upgrade is known to be buggy, and routinely ignores options and environment variables. AI also suggested that I try setting an environment variable for the alternate cache location, making sure to use sudo -E to pass it to do-release-upgrade. This turned out not to work either. Although it could have been due to the possibility that do-release-upgrade simplistically only checks the root partition free space, ignoring the lessened requirements due to relocating the cache. Once, I thought I would be lost in such a complex situation without AI, but alas, it’s final suggestion to recover space by compressing logs, removing temporary upgrade files and old snaps ended up working, but just barely. There’s got to be a better way!!!! Here’s an idea. Find a large directory with ncpd or something like that. Copy the files to USB, remove them from the root partition, and relink to the USB. This will truly reduce the space used in the root partition. The problem is that the files will be gone for a short while, and the system could go down. Is there anything that can safely be moved for a few seconds while the link executes? How about snap storage. I found this can take up a lot of space. I don’t think that the solution resides in deconstructing or fixing do-release-upgrade. Just try to work around its limitations. Might this work?

title: Ubuntu 26.04 - Session Logged out - Connected External Monitor
body: I getting logged out of the session on Ubuntu 26.04 every time when i am connecting my external monitor to HDMI port. Below summary of the tests performed: System and diagnostic results Check Result OS Ubuntu 26.04 Laptop Intel Iris Xe + NVIDIA GeForce RTX Display session Wayland Intel GPU Detected; driver i915 NVIDIA GPU Detected; driver nvidia NVIDIA driver 595.99.02 NVIDIA DRM modesetting Enabled ( Y ) Internal display card2-eDP-1 : connected NVIDIA HDMI card1-HDMI-A-2 : disconnected HDMI modes None HDMI EDID 0 bytes xrandr --query Only eDP-1 visible NVIDIA kernel log Cannot find any crtc or sizes nvidia-smi Not installed prime-select / prime-supported Not installed NVIDIA packages nvidia-driver-595 , nvidia-utils-595 , nvidia-prime not installed NVIDIA kernel modules linux-modules-nvidia-595-open-7.0.0-38-generic installed Current findings The NVIDIA kernel driver loads and DRM modesetting is enabled, but the NVIDIA HDMI connector reports disconnected , with no available modes and an EDID size of zero. The internal Intel-connected display works. The NVIDIA userspace utilities and PRIME helper packages are missing. The root cause has not yet been identified. Questions Could the missing NVIDIA userspace/PRIME packages explain the HDMI detection failure? Could this be related to Wayland or NVIDIA DRM initialization? What additional tests would distinguish a driver/PRIME issue from an HDMI hotplug, EDID, cable, or hardware problem?

title: Resolving broken linux-headers in archived bullseye-backports
body: Working on an old debian 11 (bullseye) machine which got an upgrade on Wednesday. It has linux-image-amd64 and linux-headers-amd64 from bullseye-backports , but the archive only has the dependencies of linux-image-amd64 , and is missing the dependencies of linux-headers-amd64 . A summary of apt show for relevant packages: Package: linux-headers-amd64 Version: 6.1.90-1~bpo11+1 APT-Sources: http://archive.debian.org/debian bullseye-backports/main amd64 Packages Depends: linux-headers-6.1.0-0.deb11.21-amd64 (= 6.1.90-1~bpo11+1) Package: linux-image-amd64 Version: 6.1.90-1~bpo11+1 APT-Sources: http://archive.debian.org/debian bullseye-backports/main amd64 Packages Depends: linux-image-6.1.0-0.deb11.21-amd64 (= 6.1.90-1~bpo11+1) Package: linux-image-6.1.0-0.deb11.21-amd64 Version: 6.1.90-1~bpo11+1 APT-Sources: http://archive.debian.org/debian bullseye-backports/main amd64 Packages Package: linux-headers-6.1.0-0.deb11.21-amd64 Version: <DOES NOT EXIST> APT-Sources: <DOES NOT EXIST> Package: linux-image-6.1.0-0.deb11.22-amd64-unsigned Version: 6.1.94-1~bpo11+1 APT-Sources: http://archive.debian.org/debian bullseye-backports/main amd64 Packages Package: linux-headers-6.1.0-0.deb11.22-amd64 Version: 6.1.94-1~bpo11+1 APT-Sources: http://archive.debian.org/debian bullseye-backports/main amd64 Packages Package linux-headers-*deb11.21* is not in the repository. Only linuxheaders-*deb11.22* . That leads to this output from apt : The following packages have unmet dependencies: linux-headers-amd64 : Depends: linux-headers-6.1.0-0.deb11.21-amd64 (= 6.1.90-1~bpo11+1) but it is not installable As a consequence, DKMS couldn't run, and the video drivers failed to load on next reboot, failing the desktop environment with: Sep 11 10:07:33 host systemd-modules-load[324]: Error running install command 'modprobe nvidia-modeset ; modprobe -i nvidia-current-drm ' for module nvidia_drm: retcode 1 Sep 11 10:07:33 host systemd-modules-load[324]: Failed to insert module 'nvidia_drm': Invalid argument Sep 11 10:07:33 host systemd-modules-load[348]: modprobe: FATAL: Module nvidia-current not found in directory /lib/modules/6.1.0-0.deb11.21-amd64 Sep 11 10:07:33 host systemd-modules-load[345]: modprobe: ERROR: ../libkmod/libkmod-module.c:990 command_do() Error running install command 'modprobe -i nvidia-current ' for module nvidia: retcode 1 Sep 11 10:07:33 host systemd-modules-load[345]: modprobe: ERROR: could not insert 'nvidia': Invalid argument I understand that bullseye is EOL, but: I am surprised that the archive was saved in a broken state. bullseye-backports was moved to archive.debian.org a long time ago and I haven't seen this problem before. Is it possible it is still getting updates and we're just in the middle of a transition? Maybe it's just the infrequent reboots. This seems a little too broken. Upgrading to trixie is something I am working on, but I have a lot of sites, with each requiring weeks of testing on major updates. So this can only be done gradually. Questions: What is the best way for me to ensure I don't get midnight phone calls about sites "failing to boot" (as it is perceived) on a system that is no longer upstream-supported? I see a few options: Explicitly install linux-image-6.1.0-0.deb11.22-amd64-unsigned . Repeat for headers. Remove bullseye-backports from apt sources to avoid pulling broken packages. apt-mark hold linux-image-amd64 . (Though I foresee regret when I do finally finish the upgrade). Find another mirror Wait out any transitions (which I am surprised still happen).

title: How to build a single absent in-tree kernel module with proper kernelrelease?
body: I am trying to add to my machine a 'missing' kernel module, which is in-tree, but not configured in the Ubuntu kernel builds, as discussed in this question . I am mostly following the procedure outlined in this question and answer . Specifically, I obtain the kernel source from the Ubuntu repository, and check out the tag relevant to my running kernel ( 7.0.0-28-generic ) $ git clone https://git.launchpad.net/~ubuntu-kernel/ubuntu/+source/linux/+git/noble $ cd noble $ git checkout Ubuntu-hwe-7.0-7.0.0-28.28_24.04.1 I then configure the build system $ make oldconfig #Uses config from /boot/config-7.0.0-28-generic $ sed -i 's/# CONFIG_MODULE is not set/CONFIG_MODULE=m/' .config #Enable the module I want to build $ make scripts $ make prepare $ make modules_prepare #Select relevant driver modules with 'm' when prompted $ cp /usr/src/linux-headers-$(uname -r)/Module.symvers . #Copy the current kernel's Module.symvers, to avoid rebuilding the entire kernel for generation and build the driver modules $ make M=drivers/<module> Now at this point, I could, in principle, add the modules using insmod . However, because I'm building several modules with a dependency tree, I'd like to install them to /lib/modules/7.0.0-28-generic/updates for use with modprobe . However, running make M=drivers/<module> modules_install installs my newly-built modules in /lib/modules/7.0.12+/updates instead. This makes some degree of sense, as make kernelrelease returns 7.0.12+ rather than the expected 7.0.0-28-generic . Since this kernelrelease number is embedded into the module as well, a manual copying to the normal install location will still pose issues for the use of modprobe , as discussed here . The main question is: what needs to change in my workflow to produce the expected kernelrelease value, and allow installation and modprobe use. The proposed solution on unix.se above doesn't seem to apply in this case, unless I am misunderstanding. Happy to share the exact module(s) I am trying to build if that is relevant. As far as I can tell, this is not related to the issue I'm having, and I figure a generic solution will be more applicable to others.

title: Installing Package on Offline Machine
body: I have an offline machine that I'm trying to install nvme-cli on to. I can't wrap my head around package managers. Because it's offline, I can't use apt . But I'm not sure if dpkg will work. I had a look at the dependencies and it seems like nvme-cli needs uuid-runtime and libnvme . The latter two packages don't have any dependencies that need downloading. So logically, it should be possible to install uuid-runtime and libnvme first and then finally nvme-cli with dpkg . However, I installed nvme-cli on an online machine to see how it went about installing the package (reviewed it by /var/log/dpkg.log ) but it looks like it's more complicated than I thought. It first half-installed the uuid-runtime , libnvme and nvme-cli and then it went back and configured these packages in the same order. So simply running dpkg -i uuid-runtime dpkg -i libnvme dpkg -i nvme-cli would not configure things correctly I don't think. How should I go about doing this? Should I persevere with using dpkg or is this way impossible and I should go in the direction of apt-offline ?

title: apt remove does not fail upon removing a package that is a dependency of another
body: As far as my limited experience goes, many package managers refuse to uninstall a package that is a dependency of another installed package. However, I think Apt (on Debian) is a little different in this aspect. Given a package to uninstall, it doesn't complain if that package is a dependency of another package; it simply uninstalls all those dependent packages as well. For example, I have Inkscape on my Debian 13 system. Inkscape depends on a package named librsvg2-common (it is not a recommended or suggested dependency): $ apt show inkscape Package: inkscape Version: 1.4-6 Priority: optional Section: graphics Maintainer: Debian Multimedia Maintainers <debian-multimedia@lists.debian.org> Installed-Size: 114 MB Depends: librsvg2-common, python3:any, lib2geom1.4.0 (>= 1.4), libatkmm-1.6-1v5 (>= 2.28.4), libboost-filesystem1.83.0 (>= 1.83.0) ... It's clear that librsvg2-common is automatically installed and inkscape is manually installed: $ apt-mark showauto librsvg2-common librsvg2-common $ apt-mark showmanual inkscape inkscape Uninstalling librsvg2-common seems to uninstall Inkscape and some desktop packages, among others, along with itself: $ apt --simulate remove librsvg2-common NOTE: This is only a simulation! apt needs root privileges for real execution. Keep also in mind that locking is deactivated, so don't depend on the relevance to the real current situation! The following packages were automatically installed and are no longer required: dconf-cli ibus-gtk3 libgsl28 libgtksourceview-4-0 libimage-magick-q16-perl python3-ibus-1.0 fonts-quicksand ibus-gtk4 libgslcblas0 libgtksourceview-4-common libpangomm-1.4-1v5 python3-scour fonts-tuffy lib2geom1.4.0 libgspell-1-3 libhangul-data libplymouth5 gir1.2-ibus-1.0 libatkmm-1.6-1v5 libgspell-1-common libhangul1 plymouth ibus-gtk libcairomm-1.0-1v5 libgtkmm-3.0-1t64 libimage-magick-perl plymouth-label Use 'apt autoremove' to remove them. REMOVING: desktop-base ibus ibus-data ibus-hangul inkscape librsvg2-common task-desktop task-kde-desktop Summary: Upgrading: 0, Installing: 0, Removing: 8, Not Upgrading: 1 Remv task-kde-desktop [3.81] Remv task-desktop [3.81] Remv desktop-base [13.0.4] Remv ibus-hangul [1.5.5-2+b1] Remv ibus [1.5.32-2] Remv ibus-data [1.5.32-2] Remv inkscape [1.4-6] Remv librsvg2-common [2.60.0+dfsg-1] I looked in the man page apt-get(8) but could not find any option that can alter this behaviour of apt remove . What is the reason for this design? Or am I missing something, and using Debian's package management system incorrectly?

title: Why is ssh-agent.socket restarting itself on my Debian 13 systems?
body: I have noticed that I have a few ssh-agent processes running on my Debian 13 servers. I cannot remember having configured them, so I tried to find out which component was responsible for their start. During my research, I have observed that I also have the ssh-agent.socket service running, at least while I am logged in as root via SSH. This is a systemd user service. I tried to stop it by systemctl --machine=root@ --user stop ssh-agent.socket . Immediately afterwards, I confirmed that it had been stopped by systemctl --machine=root@ --user status ssh-agent.socket . However, a few seconds later it had been started again. I would like to know by which mechanism that happens. systemctl --user --machine=root@ --recursive --reverse list-dependencies ssh-agent.socket gave the following result: ssh-agent.socket ○ ├─ssh-agent.service ● └─sockets.target ● └─basic.target ● ├─dbus.service ○ ├─dirmngr.service ○ ├─gpg-agent.service ○ ├─keyboxd.service ○ ├─ssh-agent.service ● ├─default.target ○ ├─graphical-session-pre.target ○ └─graphical-session.target This shows the four other targets or services, respectively, that might restart ssh-agent.socket . I have looked into their definition files (***), but could not identify the mechanism that restarts ssh-agent.socket after I stop it. Could somebody please explain that mechanism? (***) Some of these targets or services exist as system variant as well as user variant. In such cases, I have looked into both definition files.

title: How to analyze output of systemd dependency graph
body: What is the correct method to analyze the dependency graph produced by systemd-analyze dot ? I want all journal logs, so /var/log to be stored persistently on a separate partition and make / read only. But I run into the situation that systemd tries to mount before the mmc device is ready, and the mount service times out. I have described that issue in more detail in this post . I wanted to test if I could somehow add a service just to delay the start of journaling, allowing udev and mmc devices more time to settle. For that I need to know the order in which services are started by systemd. To get the dependency graph I did: systemd-analyze dot > depend.dot dot -Tsvg depend.dot -o depend.svg I converted the dot file to a svg but the resulting graphic is very complicated. What is the best way to analyze such a graph? Is there a better way to convert the dot file for a better visualization? I am mainly interested in a way to analyze the order in which services are started.

title: Looking for Ubuntu repo for re-installing Jammy update-manager
body: Please read "UPDATE", below, to see why the referenced article ( How do I restore the default repositories? ) does not answer my question. On my Jammy-based system (22.04), I messed up and completely hosed the Update Manager (long story). I then purged all references in apt to any packages related to Update Manager, and I'm now trying to re-install a fresh copy of the Jammy Update Uanager. However, no matter which "apt", "apt-get", and "aptitude" commands that I've used, I am getting no installation candidate for update-manager-core nor for any other related packages. Could anyone point me to an Ubuntu apt repo for Jammy from which I could re-install Update Manager? I think that with the correct repo, I could indeed perform this re-install. UPDATE : With regard to the "How do I restore the default repositories?" thread mentioned in a comment, I have already tried this, but it doesn't work for me, because the way I hosed my system involved accidentally doing a partial upgrade to "Noble" (I think that's version 24.xx). Now, even though I did everything I could to undo this and am back to successfully running Jammy software, applications, and services, the "Software Sources" window of "software-properties-gtk" shows the "base" as "noble" instead of "jammy". No matter which software source I choose, my system still thinks that my "base" is "noble", and "Update Manager" doesn't work. FURTHER UPDATE : OOPS! I wrote here that no python3 packages are installed, but I accidentally entered a typo when searching for it. The python3 packages are indeed installed, and they're all based on "python 3.12.3-0ubuntu". I tried to remove them so that I could downgrade, but they aren't in the standard repo. I searched on line and found a list of repos here which contain these python3 packages: https://packages.ubuntu.com/jammy-updates/all/update-manager-core/download However, none of these repos are signed, and apt won't use them. No keys are listed for any of these repos, so I can't add the keys for "apt-key" nor for the newer "gpg"-based signer.

title: What does dd if=/dev/mtd0 bs=1M count=1 2>/dev/null | wc -c do?
body: I'm having issues booting DietPi from an NVMe after updating SPI U-Boot on my Rock 5b and found this existing issue where OP verified that the bootloader was installed correctly with those two commands: dpkg -l | grep linux-u-boot-rock64-current dd if=/dev/mtd0 bs=1M count=1 2>/dev/null | wc -c I know that dpkg -l lists all installed packages and grep limits it to the specified line, so I was able to adjust it for my case to dpkg -l | grep linux-u-boot-rock-5b-vendor with the result being ii linux-u-boot-rock-5b-vendor 26.02.0-trunk-dietpi1 arm64 Das U-Boot for rock-5b I also know that dd if=/dev/mtd0 of=/dev/null bs=1M count=1 reads data from /dev/mtd0 and writes it to /dev/null while count=1 limits it to 1 megabyte due to the block size being set to 1M with bs=1M and that wc counts the number of lines. However, the command is written differently ( 2> instead of of= ) and there is one part which I don't understand ( -c ). Since I don't want to run a command that I don't fully understand, and it might not even work for my case since I want to boot from an NVMe not USB, and I'm on a Rock 5b not Rock64, it would be nice if someone could explain to me what exactly the full command does and whether I need to replace /dev/mtd0 with something else to verify that the bootloader was installed correct.

title: Eliminating unwanted warnings that are printed in a certain instance of running "aptitude upgrade"?
body: I completely removed all snap capabilities from my Ubuntu 22.04 host. And I also completely uninstalled the apt -based cups and its apt -based supporting packages, because I get much better printing results on my HP printer from installing and using hplip . Everything is working well, except for an extremely small issue when running aptitude : Since some standard Ubuntu packages have dependencies on cups , whenever any of those packages get upgraded via the aptitude gui or via the command-line invocation of aptitude upgrade , I get the following list of warnings: dpkg: warning: files list file for package 'cups-browsed' missing; assuming package has no files currently installed dpkg: warning: files list file for package 'cpdb-backend-cups' missing; assuming package has no files currently installed dpkg: warning: files list file for package 'cups-filters-core-drivers' missing; assuming package has no files currently installed dpkg: warning: files list file for package 'python3-cupshelpers' missing; assuming package has no files currently installed dpkg: warning: files list file for package 'python3-cups:amd64' missing; assuming package has no files currently installed dpkg: warning: files list file for package 'libcupsfilters-dev:amd64' missing; assuming package has no files currently installed dpkg: warning: files list file for package 'libnet-cups-perl' missing; assuming package has no files currently installed dpkg: warning: files list file for package 'cups-pk-helper' missing; assuming package has no files currently installed dpkg: warning: files list file for package 'cups-filters' missing; assuming package has no files currently installed dpkg: warning: files list file for package 'libcupsfilters1:amd64' missing; assuming package has no files currently installed Is there any way that I can disable these warnings from showing up? Yes, I do indeed know that they are just warnings, and that the package upgrade procedure works well. I'm just wondering whether there is some way to keep those warnings from being printed. And also, yes, I know that I could write a wrapper program for running the command-line invocation of aptitude which could filter out those warnings. But even that program could not block those warnings when the upgrade is being performed by the aptitude gui. And furthermore, yes, I do know that I could switch to apt or apt-get to do upgrades, but I prefer to use aptitude . Again, I consider this to be an extremely small issue. So if it turns out that there is no solution, I can indeed live with that, and I then will totally abandon this question. I'm just being nit-picky about what I see on my screen when I run my preferred package manager, aptitude . :)

title: How unsafe is it to always update, upgrade, and autoremove?
body: I am using Ubuntu for many years now and feel relatively safe that I could recover from weirder mistakes/problems as well (with the help of this forum e.g.). However, over the time some relatives and friends have also begun using Ubuntu, initially with my help. Can I just tell them to run sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade && sudo apt autoremove once a week? (potentially with the -y flags) What are the problems that could come up? As far as I understand autoremove always keeps a "backup" kernel as well. These are regular users, they are doing nothing special like managing a server, it's only their private machines.

title: apt-get autoremove during Debian 13 upgrade removed packages I need - how to get them back?
body: To upgrade from Debian 12 with KDE to Debian 13, I did run sudo apt-get full-upgrade -o dir::cache::archives=dir and sudo apt-get --fix-broken install -o dir::cache::archives=dir but despite of selecting a dir with more than enough disk space on it to prevent the upgrade to break, it did break in between because the root partition didn't have enough disk space or something. (I wonder whether the Debian upgrade will ever become user-friendly and properly prevent disk space issues.) When running a --fix-broken install command, it showed me packages can be removed with autoremove. Since I needed disk space, I thought running autoremove may help so I ran sudo apt-get autoremove afterwards and in /var/log/apt/history.log it shows me which packages got removed. Now I noticed that command must have removed some packages I need: Audio doesn't work anymore (no output device) Kwrite wasn't installed anymore K3B wasn't installed anymore When I open a new tab in the Konsole, it shows some errors about locale settings ( setlocale: LC_CTYPE: etc) I can't change a file in /etc/apt/sources.list.d because it fails at saving it (it takes long to show the password prompt and then it has errors in the console without saving it) Open apps are not showing in the Plasma taskbar anymore I have the mentioned history.log file and before I made the distro upgrade, I ran dpkg --get-selections > ~/dir/package-selections-$(date +%Y%m%d).txt so I also have a list of packages installed earlier. How to fix all those package problems probably introduced by the autoremove command?

title: Ubuntu default Firefox app won't start after system changes
body: First question, I'm new to this site so apologies if it's an old chestnut. I recently got pop-up warnings from the OS (Ubuntu 22.04) telling me that the root filesystem (/, mounted on /dev/sda1) was running low on disc space. I copied /home (the major culprit) to another internal disk which had plenty of free space and deleted /home from the boot disk. I then made a soft link from a new /home on /dev/sda1 to the copy of /home on the other disk. Things mostly work OK but when I try to start Firefox I get: robin~$cannot perform operation: mount --rbind /home /tmp/snap.rootfs_G5r0Tf//home: Permission denied I've done some research and it looks like this is something to do Firefox being a snap package. I've read a number of complaints about 'Permission denied' errors with snap. I'm probably going to upgrade my computer and start again with a fresh Linux (of some flavour) install, but I'd be grateful if anyone could shed light on what's going here and if possible suggest a workaround with my current setup. Robin

title: Desktop files / taskbar icons for portable applications
body: I have several GUI applications that are not shipped via Ubuntus package infrastructure, but via a 3rd party package manager ( conan ). The versions of these applications are short-lived, and the customers are frequently changing storage locations, including placing the portable applications on removable drives etc. While I have proper control over the window icon of those applications, the customers complain that in a Unitity7 and Gnome 3 based desktop, the task bar icons are always rendered as gear wheels (place holder icon). I know that I could generate a .desktop file for an application that is permanently installed in the system and place it into one of the standard paths, but that's quite a bad mismatch for the customers workflow. I do not need, nor does the customer want, a menu entry to start the application nor does "pinning" the applications to the launcher make sense in any form. Only a way to make the window properly identifiable in the task bar while running without leaving any permanent artifacts in the system. So: How can I make the default Unitity7 / Gnome 3 desktop associate a user-defined icon (instead of the default placeholder) with a window in the taskbar, without having to install .desktop files?

title: Am I required to search for the locations of all the user configuration files when I want to uninstall a program/app?
body: I've been a user of Linux for a while now, and I still can't get used to this philosophy. I want to uninstall an app/program, right? So I do: sudo apt purge an_app then: sudo apt autoremove Right. So my understanding is that the reason we do purge instead of remove is that it also deletes any configuration files. But then I asked an LLM how to remove VSCode and it tells me that I also need to remove recursively the folders: ~/.vscode ~/.config/Code And if I didn't have access to an LLM that knows everything how am I supposed to remove the files that are installed by an app? There is no way of having 'simple' setup like on Android or Windows or basically anything else that's actually convenient for the user, you know, like 'uninstall' that doesn't require you to search for all the folders that the app may have put configuration or cache files in? I'm know that nothing is perfect. For example on Windows after an uninstall you may still end up with remaining files in your Users folder, but generally it works. How are you supposed to do this on Linux. Edit: Also, am I supposed to search in .cache also?

title: How to disable netplan.io and use NetworkManager alone?
body: I'm a happy user of NetworkManager on Debian, Fedora, Arch Linux, and RHEL. I'm also using the Ansible linux-system-roles/network role to configure network bonds, bridges, etc. with NetworkManager. Unfortunately, in the past I had some issues with this approach on Ubuntu. For example, I found that some IPv6 privacy and bridge options that I applied with NetworkManager did not persist after a reboot, as Netplan overwrote them. I don't want to use Netplan as an additional abstraction layer, so I usually just uninstalled it instead of figuring out how to solve problems with Netplan. However, since 23.10, netplan.io seems to be a dependency of network-manager : # apt remove netplan.io Reading package lists... Done Building dependency tree... Done Reading state information... Done The following packages will be REMOVED: netplan.io network-manager network-manager-pptp How do I completely disable any Netplan components on recent Ubuntu versions and switch to pure NetworkManager for network configuration? I want to keep configuring networking the same way I do on my other Linux distributions and not risk introducing an unused abstraction layer. For reference, I'm trying this now on Ubuntu Server 24.04.1 LTS (Noble Numbat). I have checked other threads like this one , but I could not find any mentions on how to get rid of Netplan on recent Ubuntu versions, without also removing Networkmanager.

title: Why can the Linux device tree compiler not resolve this label for an alias?
body: Problem I am trying to add a Linux device tree alias for a network adapter, so U-Boot can assign a static MAC address to it. However, when compiling the kernel, it fails at the adjusted device tree with this error message: ERROR (path_references): /aliases: Reference to non-existent node or label "r8125_u40" It is about a device tree for the FriendlyELEC NanoPi R6S, based on mainline Linux 6.12: https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/tree/arch/arm64/boot/dts/rockchip/rk3588s-nanopi-r6s.dts?h=linux-6.12.y Relevant include: https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/tree/arch/arm64/boot/dts/rockchip/rk3588-base.dtsi?h=linux-6.12.y What I am adding to/merging into rk3588s-nanopi-r6s.dts is the following: aliases { ethernet1 = &r8125_u25; ethernet2 = &r8125_u40; }; &pcie2x1l1 { pcie@0,0 { reg = <0x00300000 0 0 0 0>; #address-cells = <3>; #size-cells = <2>; r8125_u25: pcie@30,0 { reg = <0 0 0 0 0>; local-mac-address = [ 00 00 00 00 00 00 ]; }; }; }; &pcie2x1l2 { pcie@0,0 { reg = <0x00400000 0 0 0 0>; #address-cells = <3>; #size-cells = <2>; r8125_u40: pcie@40,0 { reg = <0 0 0 0 0>; local-mac-address = [ 00 00 00 00 00 00 ]; }; }; }; Those are two PCIe network adapters. U-Boot assigns static MAC addresses to ethernet* aliases, so I add the needed PCIe sub devices, give them labels r8125_u25 and r8125_u40 and add the aliases with those labels. This works pretty well for all other SBCs I applied a similar change for PCIe Ethernet adapters, and it works well for r8125_u25 and ethernet1 . However, for the very similar second adapter, the compiler refuses to find the node. What does work It works perfectly fine to do the same change with a device tree overlay, the alias then is valid, and the Ethernet adapter (all three) get its static MAC address. But I would like to achieve this without overlay. In Linux 6.13, most of the device tree for this SBC has been moved into another include: https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/tree/arch/arm64/boot/dts/rockchip/rk3588s-nanopi-r6s.dts?h=linux-6.15.y New include: https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/stable/linux.git/tree/arch/arm64/boot/dts/rockchip/rk3588s-nanopi-r6.dtsi?h=linux-6.15.y There, (tested with Linux 6.15) patching above aliases and child nodes into rk3588s-nanopi-r6s.dts works fine. However, I would like to achieve this work current LTS as well. Solution attempts To get some quick ideas, I queried an LLM, and tried the following without success: Move PCIe device nodes to the top of the device tree source: same error Assign the full device path to the alias, instead of the label: ethernet2 = ${/pcie@fe190000/pcie@0,0/pcie@40,0}; The compiler then complains that this path does not exist. Assign a label = "r8125_u40"; to the node: same error Assign a phandle = <0x1234>; to the node: I did not find a way to assign a phandle to an alias so that it refers to the actual node, instead of just being resolved as number. Set status = "okay"; explicitly for the node, same error Apart of this, I could not find any structural difference or invalid dependency or anything that could be a relevant difference and reason why r8125_u40 fails to be resolved, while r8125_u25 works perfectly fine. I did not try to define the child nodes in a parent/include device tree source. The same kernel will be used for a lot of different SBCs, and I do not want to cause problems by defining a possibly conflicting, at least obsolete node for an SBC which does not have a network adapter attached to the same PCIe bus. Questions Why is the compiler chocking on &r8125_u40 ? What are the general rules or limitations in how the device tree compiler is able to resolve symbol labels, or even see nodes defined in the same source file at all? From what I found, it is supposed to parse everything first, and resolve symbols/labels last. Obviously a false assumption in this case. title: How to tell apt that unmet dependencies were infact built and installed from source?
body: Question: To install package A, I had to build and install some dependencies B, C, and D from source because apt couldn't install them from the repositories. Apt couldn't tell I installed these dependencies from source, so I used dpkg to force the install knowing that the dependencies were infact installed. Now when I go to install any other package E using apt, it still comes up with a warning saying package A has unmet dependencies B, C, and D. How do I tell apt to either, see that dependencies B, C, and D are in fact installed on my system, or otherwise stop showing me the warning? For context: I'm working in Ubuntu 24.04LTS on the Raspberry Pi 5. I've been trying to get the Hailo AI HAT+ and Raspberry Pi Camera Module 3 working together as well as they do on Raspberry Pi OS. This journey had sent me down a rabbit hole of building Hailort-pcie-drivers, hailort, hailo tappas, Raspberry Pi's fork of libcamera, and Raspberry Pi's rpicam-apps all from source. I have gotten the rpicam-apps demos of the AI hat working now, but having done so, apt believes that the rpicam-apps-hailo-postprocess package still has unmet dependencies of hailort, libcamera0.4, and rpicam-apps, which are "not installable" and will still show me this warning anytime I go to install another package using apt.

title: How to configure XRDP on Xubuntu 24.04 to create a new XFCE session with the same experience as a local session?
body: I am trying to configure XRDP on my Xubuntu 24.04 machine to allow remote connections from another Xubuntu 24.10 Linux machine (via VPN, same network). My goal is to create a new XFCE session through XRDP , which provides the same desktop experience as my local session , without interfering with any user that might be physically present at the machine. What I am trying to achieve I want to connect remotely and start a new session , not take over the existing local session. This new session should offer the same XFCE environment as my local desktop , including: Panels and launchers in the same positions. Desktop layout and configurations as I’ve set them locally. The same user profile experience as when logging in physically at the console. I need this remote session to start even if nobody is logged in locally . Note: On standard Ubuntu 24.04 (GNOME) , there is built-in support for remote desktop via RDP (GNOME Remote Desktop). It allows remote users to connect through RDP and either share the existing session or create a new one , depending on the setup. I would like to achieve a similar behavior on Xubuntu , where I can create a new remote session , with my XFCE desktop environment , that mirrors the experience I have when logged in locally. What I have tried VPN access is working fine. It's like I'm on the local network. XRDP is installed and running. Packages installed: xorgxrdp dbus-x11 xfce4 and xfce4-goodies /etc/X11/Xwrapper.config : allowed_users=anybody needs_root_rights=no /etc/xrdp/startwm.sh contains: #!/bin/sh if [ -r /etc/default/locale ]; then . /etc/default/locale export LANG LANGUAGE fi exec startxfce4 I also tried adding export DISPLAY=:10 in startwm.sh . I created executable ~/.xsession and ~/.Xclients with exec startxfce4 . .Xauthority has correct ownership and permissions. What happens XRDP successfully establishes a connection, creating a new session on display :10 . Xorg seems to start fine, but startxfce4 exits immediately. On the client side (Remmina RDP), I see a black screen for a few seconds and then the connection closes. xrdp-sesman.log reports: Window manager exited quickly .xorgxrdp.10.log shows the X server terminating cleanly without errors. What works (as an alternative) NoMachine Free works, but it only connects to the local physical session , which I do not want, because it disturbs any local user, in addition, there may be no active session (PC just turned on). The core question How can I configure XRDP on Xubuntu 24.04 to start a new XFCE session that loads my full user environment (panels, launchers, desktop layout), providing the same experience as logging in locally, without disturbing local users, or without having any active session? Notes I do not need multiple concurrent remote sessions. I only need one remote session , separate from the physical console. I prefer a solution that allows me to replicate the same user experience I have locally.

title: After installing Debian Sid's Nvidia 390 drivers I'm left with software rendering
body: My final goal is to make use of a Geforce GTX 550 Ti on a modern Linux Gnome desktop. Since recent Ubuntu versions stopped supporting the Nvidia 390 driver that is required for this I instead chose Debian Sid (a.k.a. Unstable), which offers seemingly straightforward install instructions for it . After trying to install them I'm left with a white "Something has gone wrong" low-resolution GUI error screen instead of the login screen (no buttons, no cursor), and switching to a console doesn't give me a login prompt, but only black screen and non-responsive caret at top left. I then need to restart and do a safe-boot to access the console. Update: After a full-upgrade I now end up with software rendering, which is technically better than having to reboot, but not much. What I've done Installed Debian Testing amd64 weekly DVD build. This was working just fine in Gnome desktop using nouveau and Wayland. Filled my sources.list with the appropriate content since it was completely empty apart from a reference to the install media (USB iso). Before that I couldn't even do an apt update . I don't know why I was left with an essentially empty sources.list immediately following a clean install. Enabled unstable by adding one line in sources.list , according to Debian's instructions to enable unstable on Testing . Followed the instructions for Nvidia 390 driver for Sid in the above linked wiki page. Yes, I forgot to install the kernel headers before doing this. Ended up with a non-working system as described above, so I uninstalled the two driver packages again using safe-boot ( nvidia-legacy-390xx-driver firmware-misc-nonfree ) and removed all three nvidia symlinks in etc/modprobe.d (one of which was blacklisting nouveau ). I got a working system back. I realized my mistake and installed the kernel headers ( linux-headers-amd64 ) according to instructions. I again tried installing the driver ( nvidia-legacy-390xx-driver firmware-misc-nonfree ) but ended up with the same result as before after a reboot. I didn't see much actual build-action going on when installing the driver packages, so I tried to --reinstall the nvidia-legacy-390xx-kernel-dkms package, which finally actually menioned "building" something. I still ended up in the same situation, i.e. no login screen and no access to console during normal boot. I'm unsure if I accidentally messed something up and didn't fix it properly, or what the problem could be at this point. What would be the best course of action to troubleshoot this situation? I also did a full-upgrade for good measure to make sure all packages were up to date. Observations When the system is working (with nouveau ), Gnome desktop works fine on Wayland but gives a fullscreen "Something has gone wrong" GUI error screen when logging in with Gnome on Xorg. It has a button to "log out" which I can click with the space bar (no mouse cursor). MATE desktop works fine though, and it also uses Xorg. I'm fine with Gnome on Xorg temporarily not working — it's Testing + Unstable after all, but I would like to think that at least the login screen ( gdm ) and console should work if the graphics drivers work (just as with nouveau )? One reason I have specifically chosen Debian Testing , i.e. Debian 13 Trixie, instead of Debian 12 is that I needed to ensure I had the very latest nouveau possible . This is because even on the most up-to-date Ubuntu 24.10 the nouveau driver will invariably freeze the entire system after some time (I have determined this experimentally; Ubuntu is locking up only when nouveau is loaded and never when running only on Intel integrated graphics). I'm trying to maximize my chances that nouveau will work (Windows 10 does not freeze, so I attribute this to the nouveau drivers, and not to the hardware). Additional info sources.list I had to reconstruct this file immediately after OS install, for some reason, because it only contained the first line (now commented out). # deb cdrom:[Debian GNU/Linux testing _T

title: How to get reverse dependencies in Debian package manager for installed packages
body: The typical way to get reverse dependencies in Debian or Debian based systems, is to either use apt-cache rdepends PackageName OR apt-cache showpkg PackageName There are two issues with this. Firstly it lists all the reverse dependencies of a package, regardless of whether the dependency is Depends, Suggests, Recommends. Secondly it does not check if the dependent package is already installed or not on the system. For example let us consider the package graphviz . Looking at its reverse dependencies we can see that there are packages like gimp and qvge (i.e. Qt Visual Graph Editor) which depend on graphviz . i.e. without graphviz installed on the system these cannot work. However there are also packages which only suggest or recommends graphviz to be installed like travis (i.e. trajectory analyzer and visualizer), webdruid and others. These packages do not require graphviz to be installed. Rather they will function just fine without graphviz . So how is it possible to find the reverse dependencies of a package in which the type of dependency is "Depends", not Suggests nor Recommends and also to list only those packages which are installed? Taking the above example how is it possible to list only gimp, qvge, plus other packages for graphviz while omit packages like travis and webdruid?

And of course there are lots of installed packages whose purpose I am completely in the dark on. So, what all can I safely remove? Or, how can I find out what I can safely remove, to minimize how much space is taken up just supporting the OS and Gnome environment, and maximize the space available for user data and programs?

title: What is the expected size of a single distribution Ubuntu Repository Mirror?
body: I've recently set up a homelab and now that I finally have plenty of storage I decided it might be a good idea to keep a copy of the Ubuntu packages for a single LTS release. In particular, I decided to mirror 24.04 Noble. Ideally, the goal is to be able to install packages and fresh ubuntu installs using my mirror, and only occasionally updates (most of my machines aren't connected to the external network) when I can update the mirror (maybe once a month or so). I also just thought it would be a fun learning experience. I followed some guides to the best of my ability and did some of my own reading, and settled on using debmirror with the following script in a docker container to perform the mirroring operation: #!/bin/bash SECTIONS="main,restricted,universe,multiverse" RELEASE="noble,noble-security,noble-updates,noble-backports" PROTO="rsync" AMD64_ARCHES="amd64" AMD64_ROOT="ubuntu" AMD64_SERVER="us.archive.ubuntu.com" AMD64_DEST="/mirror/amd64/ubuntu" ARM64_ARCHES="arm64" ARM64_ROOT="ubuntu-ports" ARM64_SERVER="us.ports.ubuntu.com" ARM64_DEST="/mirror/arm64/ubuntu" # Mirror AMD debmirror --arch="$AMD64_ARCHES"\ --section="$SECTIONS" \ --host="$AMD64_SERVER"\ --method="$PROTO" \ --root=$AMD64_ROOT \ --dist="$RELEASE" \ --source \ --progress \ --cleanup \ --keyring=/usr/share/keyrings/ubuntu-archive-keyring.gpg \ --rsync-options "-aIL --info=progress2 --partial" \ "$AMD64_DEST" # Mirror ARM64 debmirror --arch="$ARM64_ARCHES"\ --section="$SECTIONS" \ --host="$ARM64_SERVER"\ --method="$PROTO" \ --root=$ARM64_ROOT \ --dist="$RELEASE" \ --source \ --progress \ --cleanup \ --keyring=/usr/share/keyrings/ubuntu-archive-keyring.gpg \ --rsync-options "-aIL --info=progress2 --partial" \ "$ARM64_DEST" I have a repo with all the code and the Dockerfile if that is important on github . According to answers to the following question, it seems like if I mirrored the entire repo I could expect to use 2.1TB of data: size of mirror repositories I expected this would be less for mirroring only a single distribution, but I wasn't sure how much less. The amount that I have mirrored is roughly 260GB for BOTH amd64 and arm64 when mirroring both, with both halves taking up approximately the same amount of space. That is significantly less than I was expecting, and I want to make sure I haven't missed anything. I had assumed most of the distributions would share packages where applicable, so I wasn't expecting a massive reduction in size from a single distribution. Edit: The following question ( What is the size of Ubuntu repository? ) also came up, but my concern is that the most relevant answer appears to be from 12 years ago, and a lot can change between then and now. It also appears to leave out the universe section, though as I am unfamiliar with the older releases maybe that was simply a different structure at the time.

title: Force dpkg-buildpackage to specify exact dependencies for some packages?
body: I'm building an app that depends on Qt6 and by default dpkg-buildpackage generates a >= dependencies for shlibs dependencies I didn't explicitly specify . So specifying: Depends: ${shlibs:Depends} Causes: $ dpkg-query --show -f '${Depends}' mypackage ... qt6-base (>= 6.7.2), ... The problem is that Qt requires the exact specific version that the app was built against in order to run. If the system has qt6-base version 6.8.0 installed, my app will install but will fail to run - how can I prevent that? I don't want apt to update my app until I have a version that explicitly supports the exact version of Qt that is available on the system (and/or prevent updating Qt until I have released an appropriate version). I know I can add manual explicit dependencies for each and every Qt package I depend on - and then update the version manually every time I build with a new Qt version - but this is going to be so much trouble. I would expect there would by an option of something like "for packages that have the text 'qt' in their name, use a = dependency instead of a >= ".

title: Where is the Systemd ordering cycle occurring?
body: I have to Systemd units a service and a socket. The desired behavior is that when I start the socket the service will start first followed by the socket and when either is taken down they should both go down. The service binds to the socket before the socket unit starts which is why I have it as a notify service so it doesn't report as started until it has the bind on the socket. Here are the files for the two Units. #rustyvxcan.service [Unit] Description=Docker VXCAN plugin Service #PartOf=rustyvxcan.socket Before=docker.service After=network.target [Service] Type=notify ExecStartPre=/usr/bin/mkdir -p /run/docker/plugins ExecStart=/home/braedon/.cargo/bin/rustycan4docker ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target #rustyvxcan.socket [Unit] Description=A network plugin for vxcan Before=docker.service AssertPathExists=/run/docker/plugins Requires=rustyvxcan.service After=rustyvxcan.service [Socket] ListenStream=/run/docker/plugins/rustyvxcan.sock RemoveOnStop=True [Install] WantedBy=sockets.target The error message is as follows. Sep 19 16:50:38 localhost systemd[1]: rustyvxcan.service: Found ordering cycle on rustyvxcan.socket/start Sep 19 16:50:38 localhost systemd[1]: rustyvxcan.service: Found dependency on rustyvxcan.service/start Sep 19 16:50:38 localhost systemd[1]: rustyvxcan.service: Unable to break cycle starting with rustyvxcan.service/start Sep 19 16:55:09 localhost systemd[1]: rustyvxcan.socket: Found ordering cycle on rustyvxcan.service/start Sep 19 16:55:09 localhost systemd[1]: rustyvxcan.socket: Found dependency on rustyvxcan.socket/start Sep 19 16:55:09 localhost systemd[1]: rustyvxcan.socket: Unable to break cycle starting with rustyvxcan.socket/start From the resources I seem it means the cycle is only happening with these two files and I can clear the error by removing the After line from the .socket file but then they boot simultaneously and the executable for the service fails. I could probably resolve this simply by adding a sleep to the socket however I don't see enough dependency information here to cause a cycle. I have tried clearing out /{lib,etc}/systemd/system of the service and socket file and reinstalling the ones pasted here just to make sure older versions weren't running, and of course running systemctl daemon-reload regularly while modifying it. But I cant seem to figure out why specifying after breaks the dependency graph even after stripping out dependencies from the service file. Where is the loop happening that I am missing?

title: Why would apt fail to login using conf file information in auth.conf.d?
body: Quite a tricky problem, this one: I've set up a custom Debian repository on a remote server (let's say, example.com ), which is served at https://example.com/aptrepos , and for that path I've set up apache2 Basic Auth, so it requires login/password. Then, there are two Raspberry Pi 4 devices, at different locations (let's call them rpi1 and rpi2); I'm reasonably sure both of them have Debian (that is Raspbian, or Raspberry Pi OS) version bookworm , that is: $ lsb_release -a No LSB modules are available. Distributor ID: Debian Description: Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm) Release: 12 Codename: bookworm On both of them, I have created these two files: /etc/apt/sources.list.d/example-com.list , with contents: deb [trusted=yes] https://example.com/aptrepos bookworm main /etc/apt/auth.conf.d/example-com.conf , with contents: machine example.com login userx password uSeRx.PaSsWoRd ( userx is of course a stand-in for the respective users on the server, let's say user1 and user2 , and uSeRx.PaSsWoRd a stand-in for the respective passwords) I have ensured that the authentication login/passwords are correct, by trying to open e.g. https://example.com/aptrepos/dists/bookworm/Release in a web browser, and then copy/pasting the login/passwords from the respective example-com.conf files, in the browser "sign in" prompt Username/Password field which appears when this link is first opened in the browser - this works fine on respective RPi devices at both location. Now here is the problem: when I did this setup on the rpi1 device, I just ran sudo apt update afterwards, and it completed without a problem - and afterwards I could immediately do sudo apt install custom_package , and it would install the corresponding package from the custom Debian repo at https://example.com/aptrepos . If I check in Apache2 access.log on the example.com server, I see entries like: 172.16.0.1 - user1 [14/Aug/2024:11:29:55 +0000] "GET /aptrepos/dists/bookworm/Release HTTP/1.1" 304 202 "-" "Debian APT-HTTP/1.3 (2.6.1)" ... that is, there the authenticated username is given on the log line, and server responded with HTTP status code 304 (Not Modified), which is OK. But, when I tried to do sudo apt update on the other device (rpi2), it failed - don't have the exact error message by hand, but it was something like "Unauthorized access"; and obviously, I cannot install packages from the custom repo. When I look in apache2 access.log, I see: 173.16.1.49 - - [14/Aug/2024:09:11:09 +0000] "GET /aptrepos/dists/bookworm/Release HTTP/1.1" 401 1134 "-" "Debian APT-HTTP/1.3 (2.6.1)" We can now also confirm that the user agent signature on this second RPi device is the same as on the first RPi device ("Debian APT-HTTP/1.3 (2.6.1)"). So, there is no username in this log entry, and the server answered with 401 (Unauthorized) - which is the reason for sudo apt update failing on that device. title: Strange .deb dependency-problem in Linux Mint 22
body: I've come across a puzzling problem after upgrading Linux Mint from version 21.3 to 22. This is a HUGE upgrade, that probably updates every single package on the system. The upgrade went well and took a long time, of course. Afterwards I found maybe 15-20 packages that were 'orphaned', meaning that no other installed package depend on them. The can normally be removed without any problem, if they are libraries for example. So I did that as I normally do. But I'm stuck with 3 of these orphaned packages, that can't be removed without causing problems. One such package is: gir1.2-freedesktop If I try to uninstall this package, I get the following error: Some packages could not be installed. This may mean that you have requested an impossible situation or if you are using the unstable distribution that some required packages have not yet been created or been moved out of Incoming. The following information may help to resolve the situation: The following packages have unmet dependencies: mintsources : Depends: mint-common (>= 2) but it is not going to be installed Depends: gir1.2-gtk-3.0 but it is not going to be installed Depends: gir1.2-pango-1.0 but it is not going to be installed Depends: gir1.2-vte-2.91 but it is not going to be installed Depends: gir1.2-xapp-1.0 but it is not going to be installed E: Error, pkgProblemResolver::Resolve generated breaks, this may be caused by held packages. After investigating I find, that the 'orphaned' package gir1.2-freedesktop contains a number of 'virtual' packages. And other packages in the system depend on them, for example mintsources . I should mention that the commands apt-get check (Checks the system for unmet dependencies) apt install -f (Attempts to fix unmet dependencies by installing missing packages) Do not generate any suggestions, everything seems dandy. So the package systems 'seems' to be ok. Using the more thorough aptitude tool doesn't help. If I do a aptitude purge gir1.2-freedesktop it simply shows me the dependencies of all the before mentioned virtual packages and suggest, that I should NOT remove gir1.2-freedesktop . Which I haven't of course. So, how can this gir1.2-freedesktop package be marked as 'orphaned', when other packages clearly depend on its content? This suggest, that the package database is somehow not in a well-defined state. I've tried reinstalling gir1.2-freedesktop and mintsources with apt install --reinstall mintsources but to no avail. Has anyone got an idea about, how to clean this mess up? My system is working fine, but this situation puzzles me...

title: How to get information what launched a transient systemd unit?
body: I wanted to have a custom service unit depend on a mounting point of a remote filesystem CVMFS. The remote filesystem has a strange setup in systemd which I do not completely understand. I have made a simple workaround with an intermediate service unit, so it works fine. But I would like to understand how the units of the remote filesystem work, in order to be aware of such behavior in systemd. Here is the mounting point unit of the remote filesystem: $ systemctl status cvmfs-sft.cern.ch.mount * cvmfs-sft.cern.ch.mount Loaded: loaded Active: active (mounted) since Wed 2024-07-31 23:31:49 CEST; 1min 32s ago Until: Wed 2024-07-31 23:31:49 CEST; 1min 32s ago Where: /cvmfs/sft.cern.ch What: cvmfs2 It does not list a unit file . The unit must have been created somehow dynamically. So, when I add a Requires=cvmfs-sft.cern.ch.mount to my unit, it fails during the Linux boot up with this: localhost systemd[1]: Failed to start A one shot script ... <hostname> systemd[1]: ....service: Failed to schedule restart job: Unit cvmfs-sft.cern.ch.mount not found. However, if I launch my unit after the boot, it comes up fine. I.e. the Requires=cvmfs-sft.cern.ch.mount dependency works fine when I log in as a normal user, the server has reached the multiuser target, the cvmfs is mounted and that unit cvmfs-sft.cern.ch.mount is active. What I expected is to have actual unit files for the cvmfs mounting points. The remote filesystem would take its time to mount those mounting points, and my units would proceed from there. According to the CVMFS documentation , what really manages this filesystem is this autofs.service . The autofs service runs mount points like this: $ systemctl status autofs * autofs.service - Automounts filesystems on demand Loaded: loaded (/usr/lib/systemd/system/autofs.service; enabled; preset: disabled) Drop-In: /usr/lib/systemd/system/autofs.service.d `-50-cvmfs.conf ... CGroup: /system.slice/autofs.service |-3405 /usr/bin/cvmfs2 ... sft.cern.ch /cvmfs/sft.cern.ch ... What I want to ask is what can create such units without unit files in systemd? If I have an init.d script, systemd always translates it into an actual unit file, doesn't it? In this particular case, the unit status says What: cvmfs2 . Does it mean that cvmfs2 use the following feature of systemd.mount ? $ man systemd.mount ... DESCRIPTION ... The systemd-mount(1) command allows creating .mount and .automount units dynamically and transiently from the command line. I guess you need this transient behavior for mounting points, in the case when the user plugs a USB drive in the computer etc. But can other unit types be created transiently , i.e. on the fly without a unit file? Is there a good way to find out what launched such a transient unit? In my case, the unit dependencies don't tell me anything: $ sudo systemctl list-dependencies cvmfs-sft.cern.ch.mount cvmfs-sft.cern.ch.mount * |--.mount * `-system.slice $ sudo systemctl list-dependencies --reverse cvmfs-sft.cern.ch.mount cvmfs-sft.cern.ch.mount Is there some other systemctl command that could tell you something more about the provenance of a transient unit like this?

title: NFS mixup with mounted ISO images
body: I have made an offline Debian software repository with currently 49 DVD images on my NAS. I created a single directory '/mnt/ISO-images' which contains the 49 mountpoints. I export this single directory with NFS to my newly installed Debian desktops. But I find that sometimes the contents of DVD images get mixed up as seen from my desktops (when I access DVD-X I see the contents of DVD-Y), while the contents seems OK when checking it locally on the NAS. With further testing I also found that sharing the same directory '/mnt/ISO-images' over SMB goes fine: when I browse the contents of DVD X I always get the right contents. So in summary: when I browse the contents of DVDs over SMB or locally, on the NAS, I get what I expect. If I browse the same DVDs over NSF the contents of DVD's sometimes gets mixed up. Here's basically my ISO-mount-over-NFS setup, with DVD-1, 2 & 3 for Debian 12.5 AMD64 as an example: Desktop setup: in /etc/apt/sources.list: deb [trusted=yes] file:/mnt/Repo/Deb-12.5/AMD_01/ bookworm main contrib deb [trusted=yes] file:/mnt/Repo/Deb-12.5/AMD_02/ bookworm main contrib deb [trusted=yes] file:/mnt/Repo/Deb-12.5/AMD_03/ bookworm main contrib in /etc/fstab: # NFS share for Debian repo for APT package manager Nassie01:/mnt/ISO-images /mnt/Repo nfs4 _netdev 0 0 Note that I use a single mount for the remote directory which contains all the subdirs with ISO-images mounted, so no mixup of DVD images can take place at this point. NAS setup: First I create a short named symlink, f.e. DVD_01 --> Debian-12.5.0-amd64-DVD-1.iso Then I create a second symlink higher up the folder hierarchy so I can work with shorter names in 'fstab', f.e. AMD_01 --> long/path/name/DVD_01 Then I mount the ISO image in '/etc/fstab' like this: /mnt/NAS/Install/ISO-links/Deb-12.5/AMD_01 /mnt/ISO-images/Deb-12.5/AMD_01 udf,iso9660 ...,mode=0444,loop,ro,... Then I publish it with NFS in '/etc/exports': /mnt/ISO-images 192.168.144.0/23(ro,crossmnt,no_root_squash) Notes: 'ro' makes the export read only (just as a real DVD would be); 'crossmnt' makes the contents of the DVDs (in fact: whats behind the 49 mountpoints) visible over the NFS connection; 'no_root_squash' allows Aptitude (which normally is executed by 'root') to access the contents of '/mnt/ISO-images'). Problem examples when using NFS v4: I present two examples where things go wrong. In the first example, where I mount ISOs for ARM 32-bit architecture (used for my Raspberry Pis), the problem is already clear from the output of the 'mount' command (to show the active mounts) on my desktop: Nassie01:/mnt/ISO-images/Deb-12.5/AHF_01 on /mnt/Repo/Deb-12.5/AHF_01 type nfs4 ... Nassie01:/mnt/ISO-images/Deb-12.5/AHF_02 on /mnt/Repo/Deb-12.5/AHF_02 type nfs4 ... Nassie01:/mnt/ISO-images/Deb-12.5/AHF_01 on /mnt/Repo/Deb-12.5/AHF_03 type nfs4 ... In this case I can't explain why AHF_01 is reported to be mounted to AHF_01 and AHF_03 while on the NAS it's only mounted to AHF_01. But given this situation I can understand that I get a different DVD contents on the desktop and the NAS. The same problem happens with another distro, a 64 bit AMD DVD collection for Debian 11.4, but even stranger because the 'mount' command reports nothing wrong: Nassie01:/mnt/ISO-images/Deb-11.4/AMD_01 on /mnt/Repo/Deb-11.4/AMD_01 type nfs4 ... Nassie01:/mnt/ISO-images/Deb-11.4/AMD_02 on /mnt/Repo/Deb-11.4/AMD_02 type nfs4 ... Nassie01:/mnt/ISO-images/Deb-11.4/AMD_03 on /mnt/Repo/Deb-11.4/AMD_03 type nfs4 ... But still, in this case the local directory AMD_03 on the desktop shows the contents of remote directory AMD_09 on the NAS: On the desktop, over NFS (incorrect): $ cd /mnt/Repo/Deb-11.4/AMD_01 ; grep Official README.txt Debian GNU/Linux 11.4.0 "Bullseye" - Official amd64 DVD Binary-1 Debian GNU/Linux 11.4.0 "Bullseye" - Official amd64 DVD Binary-1 $ cd ../AMD_02 ; grep Official README.txt Debian GNU/Linux 11.4.0 "Bullseye" - Official amd64 DVD Binary-2 Debian GNU/Linux 11.4.0 "Bullseye" - Official amd64 DVD Binary-2 $

title: SLURM job script - why is the tmp local directory deleted before archiving can occur? How to prevent this?
body: I wrote a SLURM job script to run a computational chemistry calculation using the CREST program (part of the xtb software package). In the script, I create a temporary directory on the local storage of the compute node. The files from the submission directory are copied to this temporary directory, after which I run the CREST calculation in the background. The script contains a trap to handle SIGTERM signals (for job termination). If terminated, it attempts to archive results and copy the archive back to the original submission directory. The functions are: wait_for_allocated_time: Calculates and waits for the job's time limit report_crest_status: Reports the status of the CREST calculation archiving: Creates an archive of the output files handle_sigterm: Handles premature job termination The script is designed to: Utilize local storage on compute nodes for better I/O performance Handle job time limits gracefully Attempt to save results even if the job is terminated prematurely Provide detailed logging of the job's progress and any issues encountered The problem with the script is that it fails to create an archive because sometimes the local directory is cleaned up before archiving can occur (see output below). Running xtb crest calculation... xtb crest calculation interrupted. Received SIGTERM signal. Cleaning up... Sat Jul 6 16:24:20 CEST 2024: Creating output archive... Sat Jul 6 16:24:20 CEST 2024: LOCAL_DIR /tmp/job-11235125 total 0 Sat Jul 6 16:24:20 CEST 2024: ARCHIVE_PATH /tmp/job-11235125/output-11235125.tar.gz tar: Removing leading `/' from member names tar: /tmp/job-11235125: Cannot stat: No such file or directory tar (child): /tmp/job-11235125/output-11235125.tar.gz: Cannot open: No such file or directory tar (child): Error is not recoverable: exiting now tar: Child returned status 2 tar: Error is not recoverable: exiting now Sat Jul 6 16:24:20 CEST 2024: Failed to create output archive. Job finished. I hoped to prevent this by running a parallel process in the background and wait for it to monitor the job's allocated time. This process will sleep until the allocated time is nearly up. Only when the archiving took place, the complete job script will end and thus preventing the clean up of the local directory. body: I am trying to reduce the disk space by my system, by removing packages I don't or rarely use, as well as the RAM needed for my programs and background tasks. I need the terminal mostly for displaying various things (calendar, actual time, output of some shell/bash commands, etc.). I'm using gnome-terminal right now, but this ought to be done smarter (here: more resource efficient). Mainly, I don't really need a colourful output, so I thought about xterm doing this, but I couldn't manage transferring the command(s) I'm using with gnome-terminal to another terminal emulator. The first question would be here: How can I find out which is the most lightweight terminal emulator for use with a window manager (not a full desktop environment)? Here's a code snippet from my rc.xml of my window manager openbox : <keybind key="W-l"> <action name="Execute"> <startupnotify> <enabled>true</enabled> </startupnotify> <command>sh -c 'echo "$(date)\t\tbeginning of session lock" >> ~/.lock.log; i3lock -uc 000000'</command> </action> </keybind> <keybind key="W-c"> <action name="Execute"> <startupnotify> <enabled>true</enabled> <name>Kalender</name> </startupnotify> <shade>no</shade> <command>gnome-terminal --hide-menubar --window-with-profile=calendar --title='calendar month' --geometry=66x9 -- bash -c 'ncal -C3; read -sn1'</command> </action> </keybind> <keybind key="W-S-d"> <action name="Execute"> <startupnotify> <enabled>true</enabled> </startupnotify> <command>lxterminal --geometry=40x32 -t "To Do's" -e "vi ~/todo"</command> </action> </keybind> I rewrote the code for very simple commands like the first shortcut, but I didn't manage to "convert" the second shortcut into the form of the third one.

title: APT Troubleshooting Questions
body: I recently ran into some dpkg errors will running sudo apt full-upgrade on my VM (I ran update beforehand). I don't have the error message handy, but I remember it saying dpkg returned an error code of 1. I noticed from some of the output that apt/dpkg looked like it was removing packages that were dependencies of other packages, and it said "but removing anyway as you requested". Afterwards, nothing worked. dpkg threw more errors when I tried to run a command, Firefox crashed, the VM wouldn't shutdown. Luckily I take backups before I do upgrades. My questions came up when I was researching how to fix this. What is the difference between sudo apt full-upgrade and sudo apt upgrade? I read the man pages and understand the conceptual difference. What I don't get is when you'd use one over the other. What are the consequences of removing old packages like full-upgrade does, or not removing them like upgrade does? I assume everything broke because thefull-upgrade removed packages that were still being used. Whats the difference between -fix--missing and -fix--broken? Again, I read the man pages, but I don't get when you use one over the other, or what the consequences of each are. I couldn't find a lot online about the difference between a broken or a missing package. How does using -f with apt install differ from using it with apt update? I think I know what will happen, but I don't understand it. Finally, most guides for fixing packages issues with apt contained some version of the following: Open the terminal and enter: sudo apt --fix-missing update Update your system's package list from the available sources: sudo apt update Now, force the installation of the broken packages using the -f flag. APT will automatically search for broken packages on your system and reinstall them from the official repository: sudo apt install -f. If the aforementioned steps do not work for you, you can try to solve the issue using dpkg. Force dpkg to reconfigure all the pending packages that are already unpacked but need to undergo configuration. The -a flag in the following command stands for All*: sudo dpkg --configure -a* Pipe grep with dpkg to get a list of all the packages marked as Required*: sudo dpkg -l | grep ^..r* Use the --remove flag to delete all the broken packages: sudo dpkg --remove --force-remove-reinstreq Clean up the package cache and install scripts using apt clean*: sudo apt clean* Now, update your system's package lists using the following command: sudo apt update I couldn't find many guides that fully explained why you run each step. I sort of get the picture, but I think I need someone to tie it together for me. I feel like whenever I get errors from apt/dpkg I sort of freak out and ignore them, or frantically copy and paste random commands I find after googling the problem hoping something works. I'm trying to be more intelligent about solving it this time.

title: Kali VMware Workstation crashed after upgrading and follow-up fixes. A Public Discussion
body: When I tried to update Kali Linux 2022.4 to the latest version (2024.2) I had the following errors: sudo apt-get update …File has unexpected size (47280544 != 47280534). Mirror sync in progress? But it was fixed by sudo apt-get clean then sudo apt-get update (no problem further regarding above errors) sudo apt-get update && apt -y full-upgrade then it failed around 98% to 99% to complete by having following errors when attempting to update again: An error occurred during the signature verification. The repository is not updated and the previous index files will be used. GPG error... The following signatures couldn't be verified because the public key is not available: NO_PUBKEY... The following signatures were invalid... Failed to fetch.. E: Some index files failed to download. They have been ignored, or old ones used instead.. It was fixed by the following steps: wget -q -O https://archive.kali.org/archive-key.asc | apt-key add There is another workaround which I have not yet attempted so far: wget --no-check-certificate http.kali.org/kali/pool/main/k/kali-archive-keyring/kali-keyring_2022.1_all.deb sudo apt install ./kali-archive-keyring_2022.1_all.deb sudo apt-get update && apt -y full-upgrade (after fixing) It was completed to 100% but crashed before completion of unpacking all the packages. After that, my kali system almost froze and I accidentally clicked the log out button (perhaps a reboot would fix it). The system rebooted, but before the login screen appeared a cursor kept blinking behind the black screen and nothing appeared. It was fixed and the system recovered as: Either Ctrl + Alt + F1 to F6 or Alt + F1 to F6 until appear login status in the black screen. Choose root as login Type dpkg --configure -a (this halted due to lot of errors) apt-get autoremove apt --fix-broken install reboot (this fix all after that! meaning successfully upgraded from 2022.4 to 2024.2) After Login to my Kali Machine, there were some other problems like replacement of the default Xfce desktop environment by Xterm ! Tor Browser was removed, WPScan does not run as usual, has dependency issues etc. ( which will do later) I do not want this issue anymore if I will update another Kali Linux Version like 2022.4. Are there any safe methods to upgrade? Should it be correct to type first the following, just after the system crashed? dpkg --configure -a and apt --fix-broken install, before log out ? If that is possible in the terminal before the reboot. Kali Vmware Workstation 16.X.X Pro, 128GB HDD, and 8GB RAM.

title: Sending auditd Logs to Central Server Ubuntu 22.04
body: I want to setup logging using auditd on multiple clients and send their logs to a central logging server (using audispd-plugins package). I was following a couple of guides: https://luppeng.wordpress.com/2016/08/06/setting-up-centralized-logging-with-auditd/ https://levelup.gitconnected.com/linux-auditing-system-centralized-logging-to-remote-server-9644089702fb But I don't see the logs for the client in /var/log/audit/audit.log on the central server. Here are my steps Logging Server sudo apt install -y auditd Edit the logging config file to allow listen to port 60. sudo vim /etc/audit/auditd.conf Add the following line. tcp_listen_port = 60 Edit /etc/audit/auditd.conf to have the following line: name_format = hostname Restart the daemon. sudo service auditd restart Logging Clients Install auditd and audispd sudo apt install -y audispd-plugins Alter /etc/audit/rules.d Use the following template and update /etc/audit/rules.d: https://github.com/Neo23x0/auditd/blob/master/audit.rules sudo su cd /etc/audit/rules.d rm audit.rules wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Neo23x0/auditd/master/audit.rules Alter settings to send logs to Logging Server vim /etc/audit/audisp-remote.conf Add the following to the top of the conf file. remote_server = <ip of logging server> port = 60 Edit /etc/audit/auditd.conf to have the following line: name_format = hostname Activate remote logging plugins Open the following file. vim /etc/audit/plugins.d/au-remote.conf Edit the file to match the following. active = yes Finally, restart the service. service auditd restart
